lesson.title: The Professor President: Wilson's Vision for Reform and the World
lesson.summary: A former political science professor and university president, Woodrow Wilson brought Progressive Era reform to the federal government after taking office in 1913, before soon leading the nation through the greatest foreign policy crisis it had yet faced.
lesson.body:
Woodrow Wilson came to the presidency by an unusual path. He had spent much of his career as an academic, earning a doctorate in political science and serving as president of Princeton University, before entering politics as governor of New Jersey in 1911. Just two years later he was elected president of the United States, helped enormously by a split in the Republican Party. In the 1912 election, incumbent Republican William Howard Taft faced a challenge from Theodore Roosevelt, who ran as the candidate of the new Progressive, or Bull Moose, Party after failing to win his old party's nomination. With Republicans divided between Taft and Roosevelt, and Socialist candidate Eugene Debs also drawing votes, Wilson won a commanding majority in the Electoral College despite receiving well under half of the popular vote.

Wilson entered office as a committed reformer, though his brand of progressivism, which he called the New Freedom, differed somewhat from Roosevelt's. Where Roosevelt's New Nationalism had generally accepted the existence of large corporations and sought to regulate them, Wilson's New Freedom aimed more directly at breaking up monopolies and restoring open competition among smaller businesses, at least as a matter of stated philosophy. In practice, the two approaches often converged once each man was actually governing.

Wilson's first term produced a remarkable run of Progressive Era legislation. The Underwood Tariff Act of 1913 lowered tariff rates and was paired with a new federal income tax, made possible by the recent ratification of the Sixteenth Amendment. The Federal Reserve Act, signed in December 1913, created the nation's modern central banking system to stabilize currency and credit. In 1914, Wilson signed both the Clayton Antitrust Act, which strengthened federal power to break up monopolies, and the Federal Trade Commission Act, which created a new agency to police unfair business practices. Wilson won reelection in 1916 partly on the slogan that he had kept the country out of the European war then raging. That claim would not hold for long. Within months of his second inauguration, the crisis unfolding across the Atlantic, examined in the next chapter, would pull the United States directly into the largest conflict it had ever faced.
